newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's largest union accepts new wage accord.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's largest union accepts new wage accord.

text.p: Ireland's largest trade union, SIPTU, voted on Wednesday to accept the latest wage agreement between employers, government and unions, a cornerstone of Ireland's economic success in recent years.
Acceptance by SIPTU makes it more likely that the pact will be voted through by a full-union ballot at the Irish Congress of Trade Unions (ICTU) on Thursday, analysts said.
SIPTU did not release a detailed breakdown of the vote but media reports said Partnership 2000, the fourth agreement of its type, had been carried by a margin of at least 10,000 votes.
Partnership 2000 allows for wage rises of 9.25 percent over a three-year period and promises tax reductions of one billion punts over the life of the accord.
Analysts had been concerned that if the agreement were rejected, it could put upward pressure on Irish inflation.
"It could augur for higher wage inflation as the current strength of economic conditions favours employees over employers in one-to-one wage negotiations," Riada Stockbrokers said.
"Hence it would tend to bias up the outlook for inflation if employers were to recoup higher wage demands through increases in retail prices," the broker added.
A consensus approach by government, employers and unions to the management of the economy, known as social partership, has been a cornerstone of Irish economic success in recent years.

This approach, which includes centralised pay agreements, has kept a lid on wage inflation and industrial unrest, allowing Ireland to enjoy the fastest-growing economy in the European Union while maintaining a comfortably low inflation rate.
Acceptance of the deal effectively places a ceiling on wage inflation and serves to limit upward pressure on consumer price inflation, analysts said.

"It looks like the overall vote will be carried on Thursday which is very positive. It caps wage inflation this year at 2.5 percent which is very good," Padhraic Garvey, economist at Riada Stockbrokers said.
The programme also sets targets for the public finances, aiming for a general government deficit of not more than 1.5 percent of GDP and a debt/GDP ratio of 70 percent by 1999.
SIPTU holds 70 of the 350 votes at ICTU. IMPACT, the Irish Municipal, Public and Civil Trade Union and Ireland's second largest union, has also voted to accept the agreement.
